schedules.description:
# TENTH SCHEDULE

[Articles 102(2) and 191(2)]

**Provisions as to disqualification on ground of defection**

---

## 1. Interpretation

In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise requires,—

(a) "House" means either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature of a State;

(b) "legislature party", in relation to a member of a House belonging to any political party in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 2 or paragraph 4, means the group consisting of all the members of that House for the time being belonging to that political party in accordance with the said provisions;

(c) "original political party", in relation to a member of a House, means the political party to which he belongs for the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2;

(d) "paragraph" means a paragraph of this Schedule.

---

## 2. Disqualification on ground of defection

(1) Subject to the provisions of paragraphs 4 and 5, a member of a House belonging to any political party shall be disqualified for being a member of the House—

(a) if he has voluntarily given up his membership of such political party; or

(b) if he votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs or by any person or authority authorised by it in this behalf, without obtaining, in either case, the prior permission of such political party, person or authority and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting or abstention.

**Explanation.**—For the purposes of this sub-paragraph,—

(a) an elected member of a House shall be deemed to belong to the political party, if any, by which he was set up as a candidate for election as such member;

(b) a nominated member of a House shall,—

(i) where he is a member of any political party on the date of his nomination as such member, be deemed to belong to such political party;

(ii) in any other case, be deemed to belong to the political party of which he becomes, or, as the case may be, first becomes, a member before the expiry of six months from the date on which he takes his seat after complying with the requirements of article 99 or, as the case may be, article 188.

(2) An elected member of a House who has been elected as such otherwise than as a candidate set up by any political party shall be disqualified for being a member of the House if he joins any political party after such election.

(3) A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a member of the House if he joins any political party after the expiry of six months from the date on which he takes his seat after complying with the requirements of article 99 or, as the case may be, article 188.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of this paragraph, a person who, on the commencement of the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, is a member of a House (whether elected or nominated as such) shall,—

(i) where he was a member of a political party immediately before such commencement, be deemed, for the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph, to have been elected as a member of such House as a candidate set up by such political party;

(ii) in any other case, be deemed to be an elected member of the House who has been elected as such otherwise than as a candidate set up by any political party for the purposes of sub-paragraph (2) of this paragraph or, as the case may be, be deemed to be a nominated member of the House for the purposes of sub-paragraph (3) of this paragraph.

---

## 3. [Omitted]

*Paragraph 3 (Exceptions to disqualification — "split") was omitted by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 5 (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).*

---

## 4. Disqualification on ground of defection not to apply in case of merger

(1) A member of a House shall not be disqualified under sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 where his original political party merges with another political party and he claims that he and any other members of his original political party—

(a) have become members of such other political party or, as the case may be, of a new political party formed by such merger; or

(b) have not accepted the merger and opted to function as a separate group,

and from the time of such merger, such other political party or new political party or group, as the case may be, shall be deemed to be the political party to which he belongs for the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 and to be his original political party for the purposes of this sub-paragraph.

(2) For the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph, the merger of the original political party of a member of a House shall be deemed to have taken place if, and only if, not less than two-thirds of the members of the legislature party concerned have agreed to such merger.

---

## 5. Exemption

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Schedule, a person who has been elected to the office of the Speaker or the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People or the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States or the Chairman or the Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council of a State or the Speaker or the Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of a State, shall not be disqualified under this Schedule,—

(a) if he, by reason of his election to such office, voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party to which he belonged immediately before such election and does not, so long as he continues to hold such office thereafter, rejoin that political party or become a member of another political party; or

(b) if he, having given up by reason of his election to such office his membership of the political party to which he belonged immediately before such election, rejoins such political party after he ceases to hold such office.

---

## 6. Decision on questions as to disqualification on ground of defection

(1) If any question arises as to whether a member of a House has become subject to disqualification under this Schedule, the question shall be referred for the decision of the Chairman or, as the case may be, the Speaker of such House and his decision shall be final:

Provided that where the question which has arisen is as to whether the Chairman or the Speaker of a House has become subject to such disqualification, the question shall be referred for the decision of such member of the House as the House may elect in this behalf and his decision shall be final.

(2) All proceedings under sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph in relation to any question as to disqualification of a member of a House under this Schedule shall be deemed to be proceedings in Parliament within the meaning of article 122 or, as the case may be, proceedings in the Legislature of a State within the meaning of article 212.

---

## 7. Bar of jurisdiction of courts

Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, no court shall have any jurisdiction in respect of any matter connected with the disqualification of a member of a House under this Schedule.

---

## 8. Rules

(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-paragraph (2) of this paragraph, the Chairman or the Speaker of a House may make rules for giving effect to the provisions of this Schedule, and in particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing, such rules may provide for—

(a) the maintenance of registers or other records as to the political parties, if any, to which different members of the House belong;

(b) the report which the leader of a legislature party in relation to a member of a House shall furnish with regard to any condonation of the nature referred to in clause (b) of sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 in respect of such member, the time within which and the authority to whom such report shall be furnished;

(c) the reports which a political party shall furnish with regard to admission to such political party of any members of the House and the officer of the House to whom such reports shall be furnished; and

(d) the procedure for deciding any question referred to in sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 6 including the procedure for any inquiry which may be made for the purpose of deciding such question.

(2) The rules made by the Chairman or the Speaker of a House under sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph shall be laid as soon as may be after they are made before the House for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions and shall take effect upon the expiry of the said period of thirty days unless they are sooner approved with or without modifications or disapproved by the House and where they are so approved, they shall take effect on such approval in the form in which they were laid or in such modified form, as the case may be, and where they are so disapproved, they shall be of no effect.

(3) The Chairman or the Speaker of a House may, without prejudice to the provisions of article 105 or, as the case may be, article 194, and to any other power which he may have under this Constitution direct that any wilful contravention by any person of the rules made under this paragraph may be dealt with in the same manner as a breach of privilege of the House.

---

## Explanatory Notes (Supplementary)

*The following notes are provided for context and are not part of the official text of the Tenth Schedule.*

### Constitutional Basis

The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, commonly known as the **Anti-Defection Law**.

### Objective

The primary objective of the Tenth Schedule is to prevent political defections by legislators and to ensure the stability of governments by discouraging legislators from switching parties for personal gain.

### Key Features

1. **Disqualification**: A member of a House belonging to a political party shall be disqualified if he voluntarily gives up membership of that party or votes/abstains contrary to the party whip.

2. **Exception (Merger)**: A merger is allowed if two-thirds of the members of a legislature party agree to merge with another party.

3. **Nominated Members**: Nominated members are treated as belonging to such political party as the Government may specify, but can join a party after six months.

4. **Independent Members**: Independent members (elected without party affiliation) are disqualified if they join any political party after election.

5. **Deciding Authority**: The Chairman (in Rajya Sabha/Legislative Council) or Speaker (in Lok Sabha/Legislative Assembly) is the authority to decide disqualification matters.

### Landmark Judgments

**Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)** — The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule, but held that the Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review on grounds of malafide, perversity, or violation of natural justice.

**Mayawati v. Markandeya Chand (1998)** — Held that the split provision required one-third of members to split from the original party to form a separate group.

### Important Amendment

**Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003** — Strengthened the anti-defection law by **removing the provision for split** (which allowed one-third of members to split without disqualification). Now, only merger with two-thirds majority is permitted as an exception. It also limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15% of the total members of the House.

### Current Position

After the 91st Amendment, the only exception to disqualification is a merger where at least two-thirds of the members of a legislature party agree to the merger. The split provision has been abolished.

### Criticism

1. **Speaker's Partiality**: The Speaker belonging to the ruling party may act in a biased manner.
2. **Delay in Decisions**: Speakers often take months or years to decide disqualification petitions.
3. **Loopholes**: Legislators have found ways to circumvent the law through "constructive defection."
4. **Merger Exception**: The two-thirds merger requirement may be manipulated.

### Proposed Reforms

Various committees have recommended:
1. Deciding authority should be the President/Governor acting on the advice of the Election Commission.
2. Time limit of three months for deciding disqualification petitions.
3. Provisions to prevent defection through "voluntarily giving up membership."
4. Expulsion of defectors from holding any public office.

---

*Note: The Tenth Schedule is a crucial anti-defection mechanism that has significantly impacted Indian politics. While it has reduced overt defections, concerns about its implementation and effectiveness remain. The 91st Amendment removed the split provision, making the law stricter.*

## EXPLANATORY NOTES (SUPPLEMENTARY)

*The following notes are provided for context and are not part of the official text of the Eleventh Schedule.*

### Constitutional Basis

The Eleventh Schedule was inserted by the **Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992**, which came into force on April 24, 1993. This amendment added **Part IX** (Articles 243 to 243-O) to the Constitution, dealing with Panchayats.

### Article 243G

Article 243G empowers the Legislature of a State to endow the Panchayats with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government. Such laws may contain provisions for the devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Panchayats with respect to:

(a) the preparation of plans for economic development and social justice; and

(b) the implementation of schemes for economic development and social justice as may be entrusted to them, including those in relation to the matters listed in the Eleventh Schedule.

### Objective

The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects that Panchayats (local self-government institutions at the village, intermediate and district levels) can be entrusted with. The objective is to decentralize power and bring governance closer to the people by enabling Panchayats to prepare and implement plans for economic development and social justice.

### Significance

1. **Grassroots Democracy**: Empowers Panchayats as institutions of self-government at the grassroots level.

2. **Decentralization**: Facilitates the devolution of powers and responsibilities from State governments to local bodies.

3. **Participatory Development**: Enables local communities to participate in planning and implementation of development schemes.

4. **Holistic Development**: Covers a wide range of subjects from agriculture to social welfare, ensuring comprehensive rural development.

## STATE LEGISLATIONS ON PANCHAYATS

After the 73rd Amendment, all States enacted their own Panchayat Raj Acts to give effect to the constitutional provisions. These Acts generally devolve the subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule to Panchayats at different levels.

### Levels of Panchayats

1. **Gram Panchayat** (Village level)
2. **Panchayat Samiti** (Intermediate level/Block level)
3. **Zila Parishad** (District level)

### Functional Domain

The subjects in the Eleventh Schedule are typically distributed among these three levels based on:
- **Gram Panchayat**: Subjects requiring local level action (e.g., drinking water, village roads, primary education)
- **Panchayat Samiti**: Subjects requiring block level coordination (e.g., secondary education, block-level health centres)
- **Zila Parishad**: Subjects requiring district level planning (e.g., district hospitals, major irrigation, district roads)

---

## RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER SCHEDULES

| Schedule | Connection |
|----------|------------|
| **Twelfth Schedule** | While Eleventh Schedule lists matters for Panchayats (rural local bodies), the Twelfth Schedule lists matters for Municipalities (urban local bodies). |
| **Eighth Schedule** | Languages recognized for official purposes, which may be used for Panchayat administration. |
| **Fifth Schedule** | Special provisions for Scheduled Areas, where Panchayat provisions may apply with modifications. |

---

## KEY FEATURES OF THE 73RD AMENDMENT

The 73rd Amendment, which introduced the Eleventh Schedule, also provided for:

1. **Three-tier system**: Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels (Article 243B).

2. **Regular elections**: Elections every five years (Article 243E).

3. **Reservation**: Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women (Article 243D).

4. **State Election Commission**: For superintendence, direction and control of elections (Article 243K).

5. **State Finance Commission**: To review the financial position of Panchayats (Article 243I).

6. **District Planning Committee**: For consolidated planning at district level (Article 243ZD).

---

## CURRENT STATUS

As of 2024, all States have implemented the Panchayat Raj system. However, the degree of devolution of subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule varies across States. Some States have devolved more subjects, while others have devolved fewer.

### States with Significant Devolution

- **Kerala**: Known for extensive devolution and people's planning campaigns.
- **Karnataka**: Notable for devolution of functions and funds to Panchayats.
- **West Bengal**: Panchayats have been functioning since 1978 (before the 73rd Amendment).
- **Maharashtra**: Comprehensive devolution of subjects.

### Challenges

1. **Fiscal constraints**: Panchayats often lack adequate financial resources.
2. **Capacity building**: Panchayat members may lack training and expertise.
3. **Bureaucratic resistance**: State government officials may resist devolution of powers.
4. **Political factors**: Party politics at local level may affect Panchayat functioning.
5. **Incomplete devolution**: Many States have not fully devolved all 29 subjects.

---

## IMPORTANT SUPREME COURT JUDGMENTS

### Bhanumathi v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010)
The Supreme Court held that the provisions of Part IX are mandatory and States cannot dilute the constitutional scheme for Panchayats.

### Kishan Singh Tomar v. Municipality of Ahmedabad (2006)
Although relating to municipalities, the principles apply to Panchayats regarding the constitutional mandate for local self-government.

### State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993)
Upheld the validity of the 73rd Amendment and the reservation provisions for Panchayats.

---

## COMPARISON: ELEVENTH SCHEDULE vs TWELFTH SCHEDULE

| Aspect | Eleventh Schedule | Twelfth Schedule |
|--------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Applicable to** | Panchayats (Rural) | Municipalities (Urban) |
| **Number of subjects** | 29 | 18 |
| **Major subjects** | Agriculture, land reforms, minor irrigation, animal husbandry | Urban planning, regulation of land use, public health, fire services |
| **Constitutional basis** | Article 243G | Article 243W |
| **Amendment** | 73rd Amendment (1992) | 74th Amendment (1992) |

---

## KEY STATISTICS

- **Total number of Panchayats in India**: Approximately 2.5 lakhs
- **Elected representatives**: Over 30 lakhs
- **Women representatives**: Over 12 lakhs (due to one-third reservation)
- **States covered**: All States (except certain tribal areas and scheduled areas where modifications apply)

---

## NOTES

1. The Eleventh Schedule is not exhaustive. State Legislatures can endow Panchayats with powers and authority beyond those listed in this Schedule.

2. The subjects in the Eleventh Schedule are illustrative and not mandatory. States have discretion to decide the extent of devolution.

3. The Eleventh Schedule reflects the constitutional vision of democratic decentralization and grassroots participation in governance.

4. The effectiveness of Panchayats in handling these subjects depends on the willingness of State governments to devolve funds, functions and functionaries (the "3Fs").

---

*Note: The Eleventh Schedule is a cornerstone of India's experiment with grassroots democracy. It represents the constitutional recognition of Panchayats as institutions of self-government, entrusted with a wide range of subjects affecting the daily lives of rural citizens. While progress has been made, full realization of the constitutional vision remains a work in progress across many States.*

### Constitutional Basis

The Twelfth Schedule was inserted by the **Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992**, which came into force on June 1, 1993. This amendment added **Part IXA** (Articles 243P to 243ZG) to the Constitution, dealing with Municipalities.

### Article 243W

Article 243W empowers the Legislature of a State to endow the Municipalities with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government. Such laws may contain provisions for the devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Municipalities with respect to:

(a) the preparation of plans for economic development and social justice; and

### Objective

The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects that Municipalities (urban local bodies) can be entrusted with. The objective is to decentralize urban governance and strengthen municipal bodies as effective institutions of local self-government in urban areas.

## SIGNIFICANCE

1. **Urban Decentralization**: Facilitates devolution of powers from State governments to Municipalities.

2. **Participatory Urban Governance**: Enables citizens to participate in urban planning and decision-making.

## KEY FEATURES OF THE 74TH AMENDMENT

The 74th Amendment, which introduced the Twelfth Schedule, also provided for:

1. **Three types of Municipalities**: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation (Article 243Q).

2. **Composition**: All seats in a Municipality to be filled by direct election (Article 243R).

3. **Duration**: Five-year term for Municipalities (Article 243U).

4. **Reservation**: Seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women (Article 243T).

5. **Wards Committees**: Constitution of Wards Committees in Municipalities with population of three lakhs or more (Article 243S).

6. **State Election Commission**: For superintendence, direction and control of elections (Article 243ZA).

7. **State Finance Commission**: To review the financial position of Municipalities (Article 243Y).

8. **Metropolitan Planning Committee**: For metropolitan areas (Article 243ZE).

9. **District Planning Committee**: For consolidated planning at district level (Article 243ZD).

## IMPORTANT SUPREME COURT JUDGMENTS

### Kishan Singh Tomar v. Municipality of Ahmedabad (2006)
The Supreme Court held that the provisions of Part IXA are mandatory and States cannot postpone or delay municipal elections.

### Surya Kant v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010)
The Court emphasized that Municipalities must be given adequate powers, authority and responsibilities to function as effective institutions of self-government.

### Nagar Nigam v. Aligarh (2009)
Held that Municipal Corporations have the power to impose taxes and collect revenue for performing the functions listed in the Twelfth Schedule.

## CHALLENGES IN URBAN GOVERNANCE

1. **Financial Constraints**: Municipalities often lack adequate financial resources.
2. **Capacity Building**: Municipal staff may lack training and expertise for complex urban management.
3. **Overlapping Jurisdictions**: Confusion between State government agencies and municipal bodies.
4. **Rapid Urbanization**: Fast-growing cities face infrastructure and service delivery challenges.
5. **Political Interference**: State governments may interfere in municipal functioning.
6. **Incomplete Devolution**: Many States have not fully devolved all 18 subjects.

## NOTES

1. The Twelfth Schedule is not exhaustive. State Legislatures can endow Municipalities with powers and authority beyond those listed in this Schedule.

2. The subjects in the Twelfth Schedule are illustrative and not mandatory. States have discretion to decide the extent of devolution.

3. The Twelfth Schedule reflects the constitutional vision of urban decentralization and citizen participation in governance of cities and towns.

4. The effectiveness of Municipalities in handling these subjects depends on the willingness of State governments to devolve funds, functions and functionaries (the \"3Fs\").

5. While the 74th Amendment completed three decades in 2023, full realization of the constitutional vision for urban local bodies remains a work in progress.
